power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The 𝑚-Bonacci weighted sequence space ℓ (𝑚, 𝛼)   𝑝 is introduced for 𝑚 ≥ 2,1 ≤ 𝑝 < ∞, and 𝛼 > 0.
text.formatted: The 𝑚-Bonacci weighted sequence space ℓ (𝑚, 𝛼)   𝑝 is introduced for 𝑚 ≥ 2,1 ≤ 𝑝 < ∞, and 𝛼 > 0.

text.text: It is proved to be a Banach space isometrically isomorphic to ℓ 𝑝 , with an unconditional Schauder basis.
The space is also reflexive and uniformly convex.
Its strict inclusion chain, continuous dual, and asymptotic truncation estimate of order 𝜌 -𝛼𝑁 / 𝑝 𝑚 are established.
Based on this framework, Scaled 𝑚-BonacciNet is proposed as a lightweight CNN that rescales Fibonacci-Net channels using the dominant 𝑚-Bonacci root and employs depthwise separable convolutions.
Tribonacci-Net achieved 96.09% accuracy and 0.9581 macro F1-score on the 15-class Brain MRI dataset using 0.85 million parameters and 0.366 GFLOPs.
Pentanacci-Net attained 95.87% accuracy on the 44-class dataset, reducing parameters and FLOPs by 47.10% and 44.48%.
Hexanacci-Net achieved 83.75% accuracy and 0.7941 macro F1-score on CKD ultrasound.
The significance of medical imaging lies in its contributions to illness screening, diagnosis, treatment strategy, and clinical assessment.
Nevertheless, the escalating amount and complexity of imaging data can lead to time-intensive manual interpretation and vulnerability to observer variability.

As a result, deep learning, notably thru convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has become a significant technique for medical image classification, detection, and segmentation, owing to its capacity to learn hierarchical representations from imaging data [1, 2].
text.formatted: As a result, deep learning, notably thru convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has become a significant technique for medical image classification, detection, and segmentation, owing to its capacity to learn hierarchical representations from imaging data <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: However, the real-world implementation of CNNs in healthcare demands not just exceptional classification performance but also computational economy, reproducibility, and interoperability with resource-restricted clinical systems.
The increased architectural depth, channel width, parameter count, memory usage, and computational cost are often associated with the performance gains made by contemporary CNNs.
Deployment on mobile devices, edge platforms, and clinical systems with constrained hardware resources may be restricted by these constraints.
As a result, lightweight designs have been created to enhance the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

ShuffleNet uses pointwise group convolution and channel shuffling [3], MobileNet uses depthwise-separable convolutions and width multipliers [4], and EfficientNet jointly scales network depth, width, and input resolution [5].
text.formatted: ShuffleNet uses pointwise group convolution and channel shuffling <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, MobileNet uses depthwise-separable convolutions and width multipliers <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, and EfficientNet jointly scales network depth, width, and input resolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: To lower processing and storage needs, model-compression techniques like pruning, quantisation, and weight sharing have also been applied [6].
text.formatted: To lower processing and storage needs, model-compression techniques like pruning, quantisation, and weight sharing have also been applied <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: However, manually created schedules, empirical scaling coefficients, or architecture-search techniques are typically used to determine the layer-wise channel configurations of these models.
Fibonacci-Net proposed a recurrence-guided alternative, where the number of convolutional filters is allocated following the Fibonacci cycle [7].
text.formatted: Fibonacci-Net proposed a recurrence-guided alternative, where the number of convolutional filters is allocated following the Fibonacci cycle <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: The number of filters is equivalent to the layer-wise channel allocation or network width, because each convolutional filter outputs a single output feature channel.

1 Such Fibonacci-based filter allocation offers an interpretable alternative to the standard channel-growth schedules, but is constrained to a set second-order recurrence and offers little flexibility to adjust the network capacity.
Moreover, higher-order recurrence sequences tend to expand fast and could enlarge the model complexity if directly employed as filter counts.

This leads us to the main research question of this study: Can a scaled 𝑚-Bonacci recurrence offer a controllable filter-allocation approach to reduce the CNN complexity while maintaining classification accuracy?

We answer this question by introducing Scaled 𝑚-BonacciNet, a recurrence-guided lightweight CNN where the recurrence order 𝑚 governs an order-dependent scaling coefficient via the dominant 𝑚-Bonacci root .
Let (𝐹 1 , 𝐹 2 , . . . , 𝐹 7 ) = (21, 34, 55, 89, 144, 233, 377) represent the original configuration of the Fibonacci-Net channel.
For 𝑚 ≥ 2, the scaling coefficient is defined as 𝑠 𝑚 = ln 𝜌 2 ln 𝜌 𝑚 . where 𝜌 𝑚 is the dominant positive root of the characteristic polynomial associated with the 𝑚-Bonacci recurrence.
The output-channel count of the ℓth convolutional block is then defined as where 𝑄 8 (•) rounds the scaled value to a valid multiple of eight.
Therefore, the raw higher-order m-Bonacci sequence terms are not directly used as filter counts.
The scaling is instead determined by the dominant root on the initial Fibonacci-Net channel setup.
The resulting order-dependent channel allocation is paired with depthwise-separable convolution in the last convolutional blocks to reduce the model complexity.
The main contribution of this work is a dominant-root-scaled channel-allocation framework for recurrenceguided lightweight CNN design.

The suggested framework is an extension of Fibonacci-Net, where an explicit channel-scaling coefficient is derived by applying the recurrence order, and a common network topology is retained for the evaluated model versions.

Furthermore, the Banach-space structure, basis properties, stringent inclusion relations, continuous dual, and asymptotic truncation behaviour of the corresponding 𝑚-Bonacci weighted sequence space are examined.
The proposed CNN versions are assessed in terms of classification performance, parameters count, MACs, FLOPs, model size and inference efficiency.
Recent progress in lightweight deep learning has been driven by advancements in mathematical modelling, efficient architecture design, and application-specific categorisation approaches.

In this work, a (m)-Bonacci recurrence bridges these research directions to offer the mathematical basis of the proposed sequence space and a systematic rule of layer-wise channel allocation in a lightweight CNN.

The present section focuses on three closely connected areas: sequence spaces based on recurrence and neural operators, lightweight CNNs with focus on recurrence-guided channel allocation, and efficient deep-learning methods for medical-image categorisation.
The construction of Banach sequence spaces from matrices generated by special integer sequences has become an active topic in functional analysis.
Recent studies have particularly focused on Fibonacci-, 𝑞-Fibonacci-, and Tribonacci-based matrix domains.
Yaying et al. [8] introduced 𝑞-Fibonacci sequence spaces and investigated their Schauder bases, Köthe-Toeplitz duals, matrix mappings, and compact operators.

text.text: Current research however mainly treat single recurrence sequences independently and do not explore the effect of a changing recurrence order on the architecture of the generated spaces and the truncation behaviour of related neural operators.
The design of lightweight CNNs is a trade off between prediction performance, computational complexity, memory usage and inference time .
Recent lightweight CNNs accomplish efficiency by tiny blocks, efficient convolutions and hardwareaware design.

text.formatted: FasterNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> proposed partial convolution to reduce the duplicate computation and memory access.

text.formatted: MobileNetV4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> used efficient bottleneck blocks, mobile attention, and hardware-aware architecture search for accuracy and latency trade-offs.

text.text: More recently, LSNet [21] combines the large-field perception and small-kernel aggregation, and ShiftwiseConv [22] exploits sparse multi-path dependencies to efficiently achieve large-kernel effects.

text.text: However, current architectures usually choose layer-wise channel widths manually, empirically or by architectural search.
In contrast, the suggested method uses a scaled 𝑚-Bonacci recurrence, where 𝑚 sets the channel growth pattern and 𝑠 regulates the total network width.
Thus it delivers an interpretable, mathematically specified channel-allocation technique without any post-training compression or architecture search.
High performance classification with manageable computational and memory requirements is needed when deploying deep learning models in clinical settings.
Naeem et al. [24] introduced a lightweight five-layer CNN for brain tumour detection with minimal MRI data.

text.formatted: Dutta et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> proposed ARM-Net, which combines attention, residual connections and multiscale feature extraction.

text.formatted: Zahoor et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> introduced a residual and regional CNN to capture tumour boundaries and textures.

text.text: CerevianNet [28] employed a compact custom CNN with progressively increasing filters for multiclass brain tumour classification.
text.formatted: CerevianNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> employed a compact custom CNN with progressively increasing filters for multiclass brain tumour classification.

text.text: Pimpalkar et al. [29] compared fine-tuned CNN and transfer-learning models for classifying normal kidneys, cysts, stones and tumours for kidney CT images.
text.formatted: Pimpalkar et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> compared fine-tuned CNN and transfer-learning models for classifying normal kidneys, cysts, stones and tumours for kidney CT images.

text.text: While these methods yield good classification performance, they are mostly based on task-specific architectures, predefined filter schedules, attention modules or pretrained models.
Conversely, we propose a unified and controllable filter-allocation technique via a scaled 𝑚-Bonacci recurrence.
Its performance is assessed in terms of accuracy, macro F1-score, number of parameters, MACs, FLOPs, model size and inference efficiency on the brain MRI and kidney CT datasets.
Another closer approach is Fibonacci-Net [7] which allocates filter counts per layer in a Fibonacci sequence and employs depthwise-separable convolutions to lower computational cost.
text.formatted: Another closer approach is Fibonacci-Net <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> which allocates filter counts per layer in a Fibonacci sequence and employs depthwise-separable convolutions to lower computational cost.

text.text: Tho approach introduces an interpretable recurrence-guided allocation strategy, but it is restricted to a fixed second-order recurrence and allows little control over the overall network breadth.

The current study generalises this notion with a scaled 𝑚-Bonacci setting, in which the recurrence order 𝑚 influences the filter-growth pattern and the scaling coefficient 𝑠 regulates the overall width of the network.
Thus, the suggested method provides a larger and more controllable family of the recurrence-guided lightweight CNNs.
The proposed framework contains two related components.

text.text: This section evaluates the performance of the proposed Scaled 𝑚-BonacciNet.
It first describes the datasets, preprocessing procedures, experimental setup, and evaluation metrics.
The resulting performance is then analysed and compared with that of existing methods across the selected datasets.
Additional experiments are conducted to examine the contribution of the model's key components and its behaviour under different experimental conditions.
The proposed Scaled 𝑚-BonacciNet was evaluated using two medical image datasets.
The first is a publicly available brain MRI dataset [30] comprising 4,479 images from multiple MRI modalities, including T1, T1C+, and T2.
text.formatted: The first is a publicly available brain MRI dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> comprising 4,479 images from multiple MRI modalities, including T1, T1C+, and T2.

text.text: By considering each imaging modality separately, the dataset contains 44 highly imbalanced classes, with class sizes ranging from 17 to 233 images.
The second dataset is a locally curated ultrasound (US) kidney dataset containing stage-wise chronic kidney disease (CKD) and normal kidney images.
The images were collected at Shivam Diagnostic Centre, Jalgaon, Maharashtra, India, with institutional approval and written patient consent.
Two radiologists, each with 15 years of experience, supervised the collection, classification, and labelling of the images.
All experiments were implemented using the Keras Sequential API and executed on NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU.
The images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels and divided into training, validation, and testing sets using a stratified ratio of 60:20:20.
The models were trained using the Adam optimizer with a batch size of 8 for 50 epochs.
The learning rate was initially fixed at 1 × 10 -4 for the first 13 epochs and subsequently decayed by a factor of 0.9 until the final epoch.
No early stopping, data augmentation, or additional image-processing method was applied.
For the 4-class dataset, the scaled variants exhibited accuracy reductions ranging from 0.77 to 2.11 percentage points.

Tribonacci-Net (𝑚 = 3) showed the smallest reduction of 0.77 percentage points, followed by Pentanacci-Net (𝑚 = 5) with a reduction of 1.15 percentage points, whereas Tetranacci-Net (𝑚 = 4) and Hexanacci-Net (𝑚 = 6) each showed a reduction of 2.11 percentage points.
On the 15-class dataset, Tribonacci-Net achieved the largest accuracy improvement of 0.67 percentage points, whereas the remaining variants showed reductions of 0.22-0.44 percentage points.
On the more challenging 44-class dataset, Pentanacci-Net improved accuracy by 0.34 percentage points, whereas the other variants showed reductions ranging from 0.11 to 0.67 percentage points.
As shown in Figure 2(b), increasing the recurrence order substantially reduced the computational requirements relative to Fibonacci-Net.

Tribonacci-Net provided the most favorable balance on the 15-class dataset, improving accuracy by 0.67 percentage points while reducing parameters by approximately 37.5% and FLOPs and MACs by approximately 40.7%.

On the 44-class dataset, Pentanacci-Net offered the most favorable balance, improving accuracy by 0.34 percentage points while reducing parameters by approximately 47.1%, FLOPs and MACs by approximately 44.5%, and the number of neurons by 25.9%.
Although none of the scaled variants improved accuracy on the 4-class dataset, they achieved substantial computational reductions.
Among these variants, Tribonacci-Net (𝑚 = 3) produced the smallest accuracy reduction of 0.77 percentage points.
These findings indicate that the preferred recurrence order depends on the required balance between classification performance and computational cost.

Unlike the pattern observed across the benchmark datasets, Hexanacci-Net achieved the most favorable overall performance on the CKD ultrasound dataset.
It increased test accuracy by 3.75 percentage points relative to Fibonacci-Net while reducing the numbers of parameters, FLOPs, MACs, and neurons by 50.4%, 45.1%, 45.1%, and 25.9%, respectively.

In contrast, Tribonacci-Net and Tetranacci-Net each exhibited a 5.00-percentage-point reduction in test accuracy, whereas Pentanacci-Net showed a reduction of 6.25 percentage points, despite their substantial computational savings.

These findings indicate that the optimal recurrence order is dataset-dependent: intermediate-order variants offered the strongest trade-offs across the three benchmark datasets, whereas the higher-order Hexanacci-Net was better suited to the CKD ultrasound classification task.

text.text: We established that ℓ (𝑚, 𝛼) 𝑝 is a Banach coordinate space isometrically isomorphic to ℓ 𝑝 .
Consequently, it possesses an unconditional Schauder basis and, for 1 < 𝑝 < ∞, inherits the reflexivity and uniform convexity of ℓ 𝑝 .

text.text: We also established the strict inclusion chain which is governed by the monotonic growth of the dominant 𝑚-Bonacci roots.
The weighted-space formulation further yields an asymptotic truncation estimate of order 𝜌 -𝛼𝑁 / 𝑝 𝑚 in the unweighted ℓ 𝑝 norm.
This estimate concerns the theoretical truncation dimension and is not interpreted directly as the number of CNN filters.
Using the dominant root 𝜌 𝑚 , we defined the scaling coefficient and applied it to the original Fibonacci-Net channel configuration.
The resulting adopted channel vectors progressively narrow the network as the recurrence order increases.
